comparison: Both evaluate the core finding of NaV1.6-Slack interaction and quinidine sensitization as SUPPORTED. OpenEval R1 covers broader claim set (C3-C4, C29-C32, C52-C63) including physical interaction evidence, while Peer R1 focuses on functional sensitization claims (C3-C4, C27-C32). Both emphasize robust experimental evidence with dose-response data and convergence of multiple experimental approaches.

OpenEval R1 includes physical interaction claims (C52-C59) using immunofluorescence, co-IP, and FRET, which Peer R3 also evaluates as SUPPORTED. Both reviewers acknowledge these biochemical and imaging data as key evidence for the Slack-NaV1.6 interaction, with no concerns raised about methodology.

OpenEval R1 includes functional consequence claims (C60-C63) that Peer R10 also evaluates as SUPPORTED. Both implicitly accept these data as demonstrating functional coupling between the channels, supporting the overall interaction model.

Strong concordance with 83% claim overlap (C5, C35-C37, C125). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED the genetic validation using NaV1.6 knockout neurons showing loss of quinidine sensitivity. Both emphasize this demonstrates physiological relevance of the interaction in native neurons.

High concordance with 69% claim overlap on pharmacological dissection using TTX and riluzole (C7, C38-C47). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes systematic isolation of INaT versus INaP components with quantitative IC50 measurements. Peer review implicitly accepts these findings as part of the functional coupling demonstration.

OpenEval R3 includes methodological validation claims (C127-C129) that Peer R14 also evaluates as SUPPORTED. Both accept these controls as supporting the pharmacological approaches distinguishing INaT and INaP contributions.

Strong concordance with 85% claim overlap on domain mapping (C67-C71, C73-C78). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED the systematic identification of NaV1.6 N-terminus requirement through deletion, fragment expression, and chimeric channel experiments. Both emphasize the mechanistic insight provided by convergent approaches.

Perfect claim overlap (C79-C83) on competitive inhibition approach using Slack C-terminus. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this demonstrates requirement for Slack's C-terminus and provides foundation for therapeutic strategy. Peer review accepts this as basis for the therapeutic intervention tested in vivo.

Perfect claim overlap (C84-C89) on clinically relevant mutants. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes maintained physical interaction and functional coupling in mutants establishes clinical relevance. Peer review explicitly acknowledges this as clinically relevant for quinidine therapies in KCNT1-related epilepsies.

High concordance with 91% claim overlap (C95-C103) on therapeutic intervention. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes robust in vivo evidence but flags C104 as speculative about clinical translation. Peer review explicitly acknowledges this as 'an important finding' with therapeutic value, emphasizing its contribution to understanding quinidine's mechanism in KCNT1 epilepsies.

OpenEval R8 addresses specificity screening (C27-C28, C33-C34) showing NaV channel selectivity over AMPA receptors. Peer R1 acknowledges this finding, with Reviewer 2 noting 'the authors show that Nav, not AMPA receptors, are responsible for Slack's sensitization to quinidine blockade.' Both evaluate as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R8 includes Slick channel data (C33-C34) showing sevenfold sensitization. Peer R11 implicitly accepts this as extending the main finding to a related channel. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED, though OpenEval notes the effect is less dramatic than for Slack.

Perfect claim overlap (C48-C51) on control experiments ruling out alternative explanations. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval characterizes this as a critical negative result strengthening mechanistic interpretation. Peer review implicitly accepts these controls as supporting NaV1.6-Slack interaction specificity.

Perfect claim overlap (C64-C66) on inside-out patch experiments. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this elegantly demonstrates that elevated sodium alone is insufficient and physical interaction is required. Peer review implicitly accepts this as supporting the physical interaction model.

OpenEval R11 includes claim C91 about NaV1.6 linking to Slack activation, which Peer R5 addresses as part of the functional coupling demonstration. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED, accepting the physiological role of the interaction in native neurons.

High concordance with 67% claim overlap (C92-C93) on AHP data from NaV1.6 knockout neurons. Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes data are from heterozygous rather than homozygous knockouts. Peer review implicitly accepts this as supporting physiological relevance of the interaction.

OpenEval R12 evaluates summary/integration claims (C105-C108) as SUPPORTED, noting these are appropriate discussion points synthesizing multiple findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific summary statements.

OpenEval R13 evaluates background/context claims (C1-C2, C9-C26) as SUPPORTED by prior literature citations. These establish scientific foundation and clinical motivation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found as these are contextual rather than experimental claims.

OpenEval R14 evaluates discussion/interpretation claims (C109-C116) as SUPPORTED, noting these are appropriate discussion points integrating literature with current findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific discussion claims.

OpenEval R15 evaluates mechanistic integration claims (C117-C124) as SUPPORTED, connecting prior literature to current findings regarding epilepsy pathophysiology. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific integrative claims.

OpenEval R16 evaluates claim C72 (control observation for chimera experiments) as SUPPORTED but characterizes it as a minor technical detail. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific control.

OpenEval R17 evaluates speculative claims about clinical translation (C90, C94, C97, C104) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are explicitly speculative despite supporting in vivo data. Peer R9 evaluates overlapping therapeutic claims (C95-C104) as SUPPORTED and emphasizes this as 'an important finding' for future therapeutic strategies. Divergence reflects OpenEval's caution about clinical translation versus peer reviewers' acceptance of therapeutic potential.

OpenEval R18 evaluates mechanistic speculation claims (C130-C133) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are reasonable hypotheses lacking direct experimental support. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these speculative mechanistic claims.

Peer R10 evaluates functional consequence claims (C60-C63) as SUPPORTED, accepting them as demonstrating functional coupling. These claims are included in OpenEval R1's broader evaluation but not separately assessed by peer reviewers.
